lead: A cloud provider sells computing at three heights of one stack. Rent the virtual machine and you run the operating system yourself: infrastructure as a service. Rent the runtime and you supply only code and settings: platform as a service. Rent the finished application in a browser: software as a service. The cut point decides three things at once — what you must manage, what you pay for, and who holds the pager when the service fails at 2 a.m. Most real systems mix all three.
prereq: You need: the layered stack from chapter 1.5, so that 'layer' and 'cut point' already mean something.

blocks.text: A service model is a cut through the stack from chapter 1.5. The layers, bottom to top: hardware (servers, disks, switches in the provider's data centre), the virtual machine the hypervisor presents, the guest OS and its patches, the runtime (language runtime, web server, libraries, database engine), and the application with its data.

The provider owns and operates every layer below the cut: capacity, patching, replacing failed parts, metering. You own every layer above it. Move the cut up and you manage less, control less, and pay in a different shape — per machine-hour, per instance-month, or per user.

The layers themselves do not change between models. Only the boundary does. The same web application can run on a rented VM, on a platform, or as somebody's finished product, and moving between them is mostly a question of who patches what.
'As a service' carries one promise: the provider does the operational work at that layer and below, and bills by a meter instead of a contract.

Infrastructure as a service rents you virtual machines, block and object storage, virtual networks, load balancers and public IP addresses. You pick the OS image, install packages, patch, harden, and decide when to add or remove machines.
Billing follows the resource: compute per second or per hour while the machine runs, storage per GB-month whether or not it runs, and data leaving the provider per GB. Chapter 1.8 covers the meter.
cost = hours × rate<sub>hour</sub> + GB-months × rate<sub>GB</sub> + GB<sub>out</sub> × rate<sub>out</sub>
blocks.where: hours is running time in hours; rate<sub>hour</sub> is the price per machine-hour; GB-months is stored volume in GB-months; rate<sub>GB</sub> is the storage price; GB<sub>out</sub> is the data that leaves the provider; rate<sub>out</sub> is the egress price per GB.

blocks.text: A rented virtual server is the standard picture: 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, a 100 GB disk, an Ubuntu image you patch yourself. Common uses: lifting an existing server into the cloud unchanged, test machines that live for a week, software whose licence is tied to an OS you must control. Virtual machines themselves are Unit 3.

Platform as a service takes code, a dependency list, environment variables and data from you. It supplies the OS, the runtime, the web server, a managed database engine if you want one, log collection, and the scaling machinery.

You push with git push or a command-line tool and get a URL. No server appears in your account. Scaling is a setting: minimum 2 instances, maximum 20, add one when average CPU passes 65 percent. The provider restarts crashed processes and rolls out OS patches beneath you.

You still manage the application: code, configuration, secrets, schema, migrations and data. 'PaaS means you manage nothing' is false. You manage everything the provider cannot know about your business.

Typical uses: a small team shipping a Python or Node web app with no operations staff, an API backend, a nightly batch job. Pricing is usually per instance-hour or per request. The constraint is that your stack must fit the runtime on offer.

Software as a service delivers the whole application, in a browser or over an API. You do not choose the OS, runtime or machine. You create accounts, set roles, import data, configure workflows and connect other systems.
Billing is per user per month or per seat per year, often tiered by features or storage. Webmail, online invoicing, payroll and customer relationship software are the familiar cases.

You still own the data and who may see it. Access control, retention and audit stay with you even though the code does not; Unit 6 covers identity. One running copy serves many customers, which is what makes a per-seat price possible.

The XaaS tail applies the same idea to one layer at a time: database as a service, storage as a service, desktop as a service, functions as a service (FaaS). FaaS runs one function per event, scales to zero when idle, and bills per invocation plus per 100 ms. It is XaaS sitting on top of PaaS, not a fourth classical model.

figure.caption: The email example: 300 students on rented SaaS cost ₹36,000 a year; one self-run VM costs ₹28,800 for the machine plus ₹28,800 for 48 administrator hours, so self-run totals ₹57,600 and SaaS wins by ₹21,600. Notice the administrator time is as large as the machine cost.

spec.title: Email cost example
spec.aria: A flowchart of the email cost example: 300 students at ₹120 per year gives SaaS ₹36,000; a self-run VM costs ₹28,800 plus ₹28,800 for 48 administrator hours, total ₹57,600, so SaaS is cheaper by ₹21,600.

examples.question: A college must give 300 students email. Option A: a rented mail service at ₹120 per student per year. Option B: run its own mail server on one virtual machine at ₹2,400 per month, plus 4 hours of administrator time per month at ₹600 per hour. Compare the annual cost of both options and state which wins and by how much.
steps: Option A, rented: 300 students × ₹120 per student per year = ₹36,000 per year.
Option B, virtual machine: 12 months × ₹2,400 per month = ₹28,800 per year.
Option B, administrator time: 12 months × 4 hours per month = 48 hours per year; 48 hours × ₹600 per hour = ₹28,800 per year.
Difference: ₹57,600 − ₹36,000 = ₹21,600 per year in favour of the rented service.
examples.answer: The rented service costs ₹36,000 per year against ₹57,600 to self-run, so software as a service wins by ₹21,600 per year, before counting the patching work the college stops doing.
examples.check:
students = 300
saas_rate = 120
rented = students * saas_rate
months = 12
vm_rate = 2400
admin_hours = 4
admin_rate = 600
vm_cost = months * vm_rate
admin_cost = months * admin_hours * admin_rate
self_run = vm_cost + admin_cost
saving = self_run - rented
print(rented)
print(vm_cost)
print(admin_cost)
print(self_run)
print(saving)

traps: Saying 'in PaaS you manage nothing'. You manage code, configuration, secrets, schema and data.
Calling serverless a fourth classical model. It is a form of XaaS on top of platform as a service.
Saying that in IaaS you manage the hardware. You manage from the guest OS upward; hardware, hypervisor and network fabric stay with the provider.
Treating any downloaded app or plain website as SaaS. SaaS is a multitenant subscription service reached over a network.
Comparing a monthly machine rate with an annual per-user rate without multiplying by 12 and without counting administrator hours, which flips the answer.

quiz.q: Name the three classical service models and state, in one line each, where the provider's responsibility starts.
quiz.a: IaaS: provider owns hardware and hypervisor, you own the guest OS upward. PaaS: provider owns OS and runtime, you own the application. SaaS: provider owns the whole stack, you own data and access.

quiz.q: Why does a PaaS user still manage the database schema when the database engine itself is managed?
quiz.a: The provider patches, backs up and replicates the engine. The tables, indexes, migrations and the meaning of the rows belong to the application, so they stay with you.

quiz.q: 500 students. SaaS at ₹150 per student per year. Self-run: one VM at ₹3,000 per month plus 5 administrator hours per month at ₹500 per hour. Compute both annual costs and say which wins.
A team moves an application from IaaS to PaaS and finds a library that needs its own kernel module. Explain what happened and give one fix.
quiz.a: The cut point moved above the OS, so the team no longer controls the kernel and the runtime cannot load the module. Fix: keep that component on IaaS, or rewrite without the module.

quiz.q: Classify each as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or FaaS: (a) webmail in a browser; (b) a virtual machine whose OS you patch; (c) git push of a Flask app that returns a URL; (d) a function that runs when an image is uploaded.
quiz.a: (a) SaaS; (b) IaaS; (c) PaaS; (d) FaaS, a form of XaaS.

quiz.q: What is the usual billing unit for IaaS compute, and for SaaS?
quiz.a: IaaS compute is billed per second or per hour of running time. SaaS is billed per user per month or per seat per year.

quiz.q: Why is scaling a setting in PaaS but a script in IaaS?
quiz.a: In IaaS the provider sees only virtual machines and not your request rate, so you write rules that create and destroy machines. In PaaS the provider owns the runtime and load balancer, counts requests itself, and needs only your minimum, maximum and a target such as 65 percent CPU.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry has split the tail further into container as a service and function as a service with per-millisecond billing, and into internal developer platforms that are a private PaaS built on Kubernetes. The FinOps discipline studies the cost line of this chapter: matching each workload to the cheapest cut point that still meets its constraints. Cold starts in FaaS and the price of egress are the two live engineering topics. Search terms: serverless cold start, platform engineering, FinOps unit economics, container as a service.
